content: Magnesium oxide can reduce the levels of moxifloxacin by inhibiting gastrointestinal absorption. This interaction is relevant only when both agents are administered orally. To minimize this effect, it is recommended to separate the administration of these drugs by at least 2 hours. Close monitoring is advised. Neomycin, when taken orally, can decrease magnesium oxide levels by increasing renal clearance. The clinical significance of this interaction is unclear, but close monitoring is recommended. Magnesium oxide can lower the levels or effectiveness of neratinib by increasing gastric pH. This interaction applies only to the oral forms of both agents. Therapy modification and close monitoring are advised. To avoid this interaction, separate the administration of antacids and neratinib by at least 3 hours. Magnesium oxide can reduce the levels of nilotinib by increasing gastric pH. This interaction is relevant only for oral formulations. Therapy modification and close monitoring are recommended. To avoid this interaction, administer antacids 2 hours before or 2 hours after nilotinib. Magnesium oxide can decrease the levels of nitrofurantoin by inhibiting gastrointestinal absorption. This interaction applies only to oral forms of both agents. The clinical significance is unknown, but close monitoring is advised. Magnesium oxide can reduce the levels of ofloxacin by inhibiting gastrointestinal absorption. This interaction is relevant only for oral formulations. To minimize this effect, separate the administration of these drugs by at least 2 hours. Close monitoring is recommended. Magnesium oxide can lower the levels or effectiveness of omadacycline by inhibiting gastrointestinal absorption. This interaction applies only to oral forms of both agents. Therapy modification and close monitoring are advised. Multivalent cation-containing products, such as magnesium oxide, may impair the absorption of tetracyclines, reducing their efficacy. Separate the administration of tetracyclines from these products. Magnesium oxide can decrease the levels of oxytetracycline by inhibiting gastrointestinal absorption. This interaction applies only to oral forms of both agents. It is recommended to avoid this combination or use an alternative drug. Paromomycin can reduce magnesium oxide levels by increasing renal clearance. The clinical significance of this interaction is unclear, but close monitoring is recommended. Magnesium oxide can lower the levels of penicillamine by inhibiting gastrointestinal absorption. This interaction is relevant only for oral formulations. To minimize this effect, separate the administration of these drugs by at least 2 hours. Close monitoring is advised. Magnesium oxide can reduce the levels or effectiveness of pexidartinib by inhibiting gastrointestinal absorption. This interaction applies only to oral forms of both agents. Therapy modification and close monitoring are recommended. To avoid this interaction, administer pexidartinib 2 hours before or 2 hours after taking a locally-acting antacid. Magnesium oxide can decrease the levels of ponatinib by increasing gastric pH. This interaction applies only to oral forms of both agents. It is recommended to avoid this combination or use an alternative drug. Magnesium oxide can reduce the levels of rilpivirine by increasing gastric pH. This interaction is relevant only for oral formulations. Therapy modification and close monitoring are advised. Co-administration of antacids with rilpivirine may significantly decrease rilpivirine plasma concentrations due to increased gastric pH. If antacids must be administered, they should be given at least 2 hours before or at least 4 hours after rilpivirine. For the combination product dolutegravir/rilpivirine, antacids should be given at least 4 hours before or at least 6 hours afterward. Magnesium oxide can lower the levels of riociguat by inhibiting gastrointestinal absorption. This interaction applies only to oral forms of both agents. To minimize this effect, separate the administration of these drugs by at least 1 hour. Close monitoring is recommended. Magnesium oxide can reduce the levels or effectiveness of sarecycline by inhibiting gastrointestinal absorption. This interaction applies only to oral forms of both agents. Therapy modification and close monitoring are advised. Multivalent cation-containing products, such as magnesium oxide, may impair the absorption of tetracyclines, reducing their efficacy. Separate the administration of tetracyclines from these products. Sodium polystyrene sulfonate can increase magnesium oxide levels by decreasing renal clearance. The clinical significance of this interaction is unclear, but there is a risk of alkalosis. Close monitoring is recommended. Magnesium sulfate/potassium chloride can increase the toxicity of magnesium oxide. Co-administration with medications that cause fluid and electrolyte abnormalities may increase the risk of adverse events such as seizures, arrhythmias, and renal impairment. Close monitoring is advised. Sodium sulfate/potassium sulfate/magnesium sulfate can increase the toxicity of magnesium oxide. Co-administration with medications that cause fluid and electrolyte abnormalities may increase the risk of adverse events such as seizures, arrhythmias, and renal impairment. Close monitoring is recommended. Magnesium oxide can reduce the levels or effectiveness of sofosbuvir/velpatasvir by increasing gastric pH. This interaction applies only to oral forms of both agents. Therapy modification and close monitoring are advised. Velpatasvir solubility decreases as gastric pH increases (it becomes practically insoluble at pH > 5). Separate the administration of sofosbuvir/velpatasvir from antacids by at least 4 hours. Magnesium oxide can lower the levels or effectiveness of sotorasib by inhibiting gastrointestinal absorption. This interaction applies only to oral forms of both agents. It is recommended to avoid this combination or use an alternative drug. If co-administration with an acid-reducing agent cannot be avoided, administer sotorasib 4 hours before or 10 hours after a locally-acting antacid. Magnesium oxide can reduce the effects of sparsentan by increasing gastric pH. This interaction is relevant only for oral formulations. Therapy modification and close monitoring are advised. Administer sparsentan 2 hours before or after antacids. Antacids may decrease sparsentan exposure, potentially reducing its efficacy. Spironolactone can increase magnesium oxide levels by decreasing renal clearance. The clinical significance of this interaction is unclear, but close monitoring is recommended. Streptomycin can reduce magnesium oxide levels by increasing renal clearance. The clinical significance of this interaction is unclear, but close monitoring is recommended. Magnesium oxide can decrease the levels of tetracycline by inhibiting gastrointestinal absorption. This interaction applies only to oral forms of both agents. It is recommended to avoid this combination or use an alternative drug. Tobramycin can reduce magnesium oxide levels by increasing renal clearance. The clinical significance of this interaction is unclear, but close monitoring is recommended. Torasemide can reduce magnesium oxide levels by increasing renal clearance. The clinical significance of this interaction is unclear, but close monitoring is recommended. Triamterene can increase magnesium oxide levels by decreasing renal clearance. The clinical significance of this interaction is unclear, but close monitoring is recommended. Magnesium oxide can reduce the levels or effectiveness of vismodegib. Therapy modification and close monitoring are advised. Magnesium supplementation may exacerbate conditions such as renal impairment or neuromuscular diseases like myasthenia gravis. Caution is advised in these cases. During pregnancy, 350–400 mg/day of elemental magnesium is recommended, and during lactation, 310–360 mg/day is advised. Magnesium is essential for various metabolic functions, including enzymatic reactions, phosphate transfer, muscle contraction, and nerve conduction. Absorption is inversely proportional to dose, with approximately 50% absorption under controlled dietary intake and 15–30% with high doses. Magnesium is distributed primarily in bone (50–60%) and extracellular fluid (1–2%), with 30% protein binding (albumin). It is excreted via urine.
